title: Oscar and the Orchard
premise: In the winter of 1899, the coastal town of Orchard's End is requisitioned by an army fleeing a continental war, and every resident must be entered into a ledger that determines who may stay and who will be shipped to the colonies. Lior Ashgrove, the lighthouse keeper who buried his wife two years ago, has spent his life being useful but unseen—until he is forced to copy the ledger himself and realizes only one berth remains for his family: his ailing sister Maren or his orphaned nephew Oscar. When Lior discovers the commanding officer is falsifying names to smuggle out deserters, he trades his silence for Oscar's passage, then burns the ledger on the last night of the century so no one else can be bought or sold by it. The novel ends with Lior keeping the light alone as the new year breaks, finally visible to everyone, at peace with what visibility costs.
about_author: Ines Almeida is a former archivist from Porto who writes historical fiction about ordinary people caught in bureaucratic machinery. 'Oscar and the Orchard' was inspired by her grandmother's stories of wartime requisitions along the Atlantic coast.

chapters.title: The Weight of Glass
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. He polishes the lighthouse lens, tends his late wife's neglected orchard, and quietly manages his sister Maren's worsening cough while keeping ten-year-old Oscar fed and schooled. The chapter establishes his philosophy of invisibility—do your work, sign nothing, want nothing publicly. Emotional beat: tender melancholy; Lior mistakes routine for safety.

chapters.title: Grey Ships at Dawn
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Three troop ships anchor in the bay and soldiers occupy the town within a day. A young officer, Captain Voss, posts a proclamation: all residents must register in the census ledger to receive ration chits. Lior watches neighbors line up like sheep and feels the first prickle of dread. Emotional beat: quiet alarm beneath enforced calm.

chapters.title: Names in Ink
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren registers the family and learns the ledger isn't just a census—it ranks residents by usefulness, and the bottom tier will be transported overseas as laborers. Her illness makes her a liability on paper. She hides this from Lior. Emotional beat: fierce maternal protectiveness curdling into fear.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Summons
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Voss conscripts Lior as the army's clerk because he has the steadiest hand in town, forcing him to transcribe the very ledger that dooms people. Copying names, he sees the arithmetic plainly: one transport berth remains unassigned before the New Year convoy. Emotional beat: complicity and shame; invisibility revealed as an illusion.

chapters.title: What the Orchard Remembers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar sneaks into the occupied orchard and befriends a soldier, Private Hale, who is clearly a deserter hiding among the garrison. Through the boy's eyes we see the occupation's absurdity—and Oscar overhears officers discussing how berths are being sold to the highest bidders. Emotional beat: childhood wonder shadowed by dawning knowledge.

chapters.title: A Price in Apples
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Voss catches Hale's desertion and offers Lior a bargain: stay silent about the falsified entries, and name whoever he likes for the last berth. Lior spends a sleepless night weighing Maren against Oscar, walking the orchard where his wife once told him love doesn't divide—it multiplies. Emotional beat: agonizing moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren discovers Lior's torment and secretly petitions Voss herself, offering to take the transport voluntarily if Oscar gets her berth. Lior intercepts the arrangement and they collide in a devastating argument where each accuses the other of playing God. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into love; the family fractures under impossible choice.

chapters.title: The Storm Before the Century
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The great storm arrives early, knocking out the harbor lights as the convoy prepares to sail. In the chaos, Hale begs sanctuary in the lighthouse, and Voss arrives with soldiers to execute him as an example. Lior stands between them, holding the ledger, and demands a final trade. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into resolve—the invisible man steps into the light.

chapters.title: Ashgrove Burns
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, climax. Lior reveals he memorized every falsification and threatens to expose Voss unless Hale sails free, Maren receives medical discharge, and Oscar takes the last berth. Voss relents—but Lior throws the ledger into the lighthouse stove anyway, erasing everyone's leverage, including his own. Emotional beat: cathartic destruction; power dies when its paper does.

chapters.title: First Light, First Year
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, resolution. On January first, the convoy departs with Hale and Oscar aboard while Maren recovers ashore. Oscar watches the lighthouse beam sweep over the water, knowing his uncle chose to remain seen and alone so others could go free. The orchard, pruned by soldiers' axes, shows its first spring buds. Emotional beat: sorrow braided with hope; belonging redefined as memory rather than place.
